title: Dha and Ni - The Full Saptak
description: Learn the last two swaras and play all seven notes of the saptak for the first time.

tasks.title: Meet Dha - the sixth note
content: Dha (Dhaivat) is the sixth note of the sargam. It sits a whole step above Pa, at semitone 9.
On the bansuri, you play Dha by lifting your right-hand ring finger (the bottom finger) while keeping the other five holes covered.

items: Pa (lift bottom three, half-hole or cross-finger) - semitone 7
Dha (specific fingering for your flute) - semitone 9

content.text: Dha is one of the five 'chal' (movable) swaras - it can be sharpened or flattened in different ragas. For now, we use the shuddh (natural) Dha.

questions.prompt: What is the semitone value of Dha in the shuddh (natural) saptak?

options.why: 8 would be komal (flat) Dha, used in some ragas but not the natural scale.

options.yes: Correct! Shuddh Dha sits at semitone 9.

options.why: 10 would be between Dha and Ni.

questions.prompt: I understand that Dha is the sixth swara and sits at semitone 9

hints: Count up from Sa: Sa(0), Re(2), Ga(4), Ma(5), Pa(7), Dha(9).
Dha is a whole step (two semitones) above Pa.

tasks.title: Play and hold Dha
content: Now try playing Dha on your bansuri. The fingering depends on your flute type, but the key is to get a clear tone at the right pitch.
Listen to how Dha sounds relative to Sa. It has a bright, warm quality - not as stable-sounding as Pa, but rich and resonant.

content.text: If you have a tanpura or drone playing Sa in the background, notice how Dha creates a gentle tension that wants to move - either up to Ni or back down to Pa.

questions.prompt: Play Dha and hold it for 3 seconds.
Now hold Dha for 5 seconds with tighter pitch control.

hints: Make sure only the correct holes are open - any leak will shift the pitch.
Blow with the same gentle, steady pressure you used for Sa.
If the pitch is flat, try directing your airstream slightly more across the hole.

tasks.title: Meet Ni - the seventh note
content: Ni (Nishad) is the seventh and final note before you return to Sa in the upper octave. It sits at semitone 11, just one whole step below the upper Sa.
Ni is sometimes called the 'leading tone' because it creates a strong pull toward Sa - when you hear Ni, your ear expects Sa to follow.

items: Ni is the seventh swara of the sargam
It is a 'chal' (movable) swara - it can be komal (flat, semitone 10) in some ragas
Shuddh Ni is a half step below the upper Sa (semitone 12)

content.text: The pull from Ni to Sa is one of the strongest melodic forces in Indian music. Many ragas use this tension to create emotional impact.

questions.prompt: Why is Ni called a 'leading tone'?

options.why: Volume has nothing to do with it.

options.text: It creates a strong pull toward Sa
options.yes: Exactly! Ni sits just below Sa and your ear naturally expects Sa to follow.

options.text: It is always played first in a raga
options.why: Ragas can start on many different notes.
Ni is a melodic note, not a rhythmic concept.

questions.prompt: What is the semitone value of shuddh Ni?
questions.yes: Right - Ni is at semitone 11, one whole step below the upper Sa at 12.

hints: Ni is a whole step below Sa' (upper Sa at semitone 12).
Think of it as the note that 'leads' your ear back home to Sa.

tasks.title: Play and hold Ni
content: Ni requires careful fingering - it is high in the scale and small changes in finger position or breath can shift it sharply.
Play Ni and notice how it feels unstable compared to Sa or Pa. That instability is musical - it is what gives Ni its expressive power.

content.text: On many bansuris, Ni uses a half-hole or cross-fingering technique. Take your time getting the pitch right before worrying about duration.

questions.prompt: Play Ni and hold it for 3 seconds.
Hold Ni for 5 seconds with steady pitch.

hints: Ni is a high note - you may need slightly more air pressure than for lower notes.
Keep your fingers relaxed even though the fingering may feel awkward at first.
If Ni sounds too sharp, check that you are not over-blowing.

tasks.title: Ear training - Dha and Ni
content: Now that you can play both notes, train your ear to tell them apart from the other swaras.
Listen carefully to each note played and identify whether it is Dha or Ni. The difference is a whole step (two semitones): Dha is warmer and more settled, Ni is brighter and pulls toward Sa.

questions.prompt: Listen to this note. Is it Dha or Ni?
Which note is this?
And this note?
Last one - identify this swara.

hints: Dha has a warmer, more relaxed colour. Ni sounds brighter and tense.
If you are unsure, hum the note and then try singing up to Sa - if it feels like one step, it is Ni; two steps, it is Dha.

tasks.title: The ascending saptak
content: This is the moment you have been building toward: playing all seven notes of the sargam in ascending order.
The ascending saptak (aaroh) goes: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa'
Take it slowly. Play each note clearly, hold it for a beat, then move to the next. No rushing.

content.text: Sa' (upper Sa) is played by overblowing - same fingering as lower Sa (all holes closed), but with more air pressure and a tighter lip opening. The pitch jumps up one octave.

questions.prompt: Play the ascending saptak: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa'

hints: Go slowly - accuracy matters more than speed at this stage.
Breathe before you start. You need enough air for all eight notes.
If you lose the pitch on Dha or Ni, pause, reset, and try again from Pa.

tasks.title: The descending saptak
content: Now play the saptak in reverse - the avaroh (descending scale): Sa' Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa
Descending is often harder than ascending because you are adding fingers back down and the transitions feel different.
Pay special attention to the transition from Ni down to Dha - keep the pitch clean on each landing.

content.text: In many ragas, the descending movement (avaroh) is different from the ascending (aaroh). For now, we simply reverse the natural scale.

questions.prompt: Play the descending saptak: Sa' Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa

hints: The transition from Sa' to Ni is tricky - ease off the air pressure gradually as you open finger holes.
Think of it as 'coming home' - each note brings you closer to Sa.
If a note squeaks, you probably moved your fingers too fast. Lift and place them deliberately.

tasks.title: Alankar with all seven notes
content: An alankar is a melodic pattern repeated at each step of the scale. Now that you know all seven notes, you can play patterns that span the full saptak.
Here are two patterns to try:

items: Pattern 1 (pairs): Sa-Re, Re-Ga, Ga-Ma, Ma-Pa, Pa-Dha, Dha-Ni, Ni-Sa'
Pattern 2 (triplets): Sa-Re-Ga, Re-Ga-Ma, Ga-Ma-Pa, Ma-Pa-Dha, Pa-Dha-Ni, Dha-Ni-Sa'

content: Start with Pattern 1 - it is gentler on your fingers.

content.text: Alankars are the scales and arpeggios of Indian music. Regular alankar practice builds finger speed, clean transitions, and deep familiarity with the notes.

questions.prompt: Play the pairs alankar: Sa-Re, Re-Ga, Ga-Ma, Ma-Pa, Pa-Dha, Dha-Ni, Ni-Sa'
Play the triplets alankar: Sa-Re-Ga, Re-Ga-Ma, Ga-Ma-Pa, Ma-Pa-Dha

hints: Keep each note the same length - evenness is the goal of alankar.
If a transition is sloppy, slow down just for that pair until it cleans up.
Breathe between patterns if you need to - there is no penalty for taking a breath.

tasks.title: A melody using the full saptak
content: Here is a simple melody that uses all seven notes. It moves up through the scale, pauses at the top, and comes back down with a slight variation.
The phrase: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa - Dha Ni Sa' - Ni Dha Pa - Ma Ga Re Sa
Notice how the melody breathes: it climbs steadily, reaches Sa', then descends in groups. This is how real music uses the saptak - not just up and down, but with shape and phrasing.

content.text: The pauses (shown as dashes) are where you take a quick breath. Learning to breathe between phrases is essential for playing real music.

questions.prompt: Play the melody: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa' Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa

hints: Break it into three phrases: ascend to Pa, ascend to Sa', then descend home.
Breathe after the first Pa and again after Sa' at the top.
Do not rush the descent - give each note its full value.

tasks.title: Full saptak challenge
content: Final challenge: prove your command of all seven notes with a comprehensive test.
First, identify some notes by ear. Then play the full ascending and descending saptak in one continuous phrase.

content.text: This is a milestone moment - completing the full saptak means you have the foundation for every raga and every melody in Indian music. Everything from here builds on these seven notes.

questions.prompt: Identify this note from the upper saptak.
And this one?
Name all seven swaras in ascending order, separated by spaces.

questions.prompt: Play the full saptak up and back down: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa' Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa

hints: Take a deep breath before the playing challenge - you need air for 15 notes.
Keep the tempo steady. It is better to play slowly and accurately.
If you stumble on the descent, remember: it is the ascent in reverse - Ni, Dha, Pa, Ma, Ga, Re, Sa.
